content: Spent the morning on the nightly stock reconciliation job. The discrepancies were not rounding: the Rotterdam warehouse writes timestamps in local time while every other site writes UTC, so anything moved between 00:00 and 02:00 CET was counted on the wrong day.
Decided to normalise the warehouse timestamps at read time rather than migrating the historical rows, because the old rows are referenced by audit exports we cannot rewrite.
Agreed the team convention: every service writes UTC and renders local time only in the presentation layer. Added a lint rule that fails a build on a naive datetime.
The invoice PDF generator runs out of memory on batches over four thousand documents. Switched it to stream page by page instead of building the whole document in memory first.
Rotterdam asked whether the warehouse dashboard could show stock levels per aisle. Purely a UI change, no data model impact, parked until after the quarter.
Reviewed the nightly job schedule. Stock reconciliation runs at 02:30, invoice generation at 03:00, and the backup at 04:00. No changes needed.

Discussed whether promised delivery dates need a time component. Decided to store them as a plain date, not a datetime: a delivery promise is a calendar day, not a moment, and treating it as one sidesteps the timezone question for that field entirely.

Customer asked why an invoice showed net-30 payment terms when their contract says net-60. Turned out the billing profile default overrides the contract field unless someone remembers to set it manually; flagged for the billing team, no fix shipped yet.

Moved the nightly backup window from 04:00 to 05:30. It had been overlapping with the stock reconciliation job's retry window, and the two competing for the same database rows was causing lock contention that slowed both jobs down.

Invoice PDFs migrated to a new HTML-to-PDF renderer. The old one silently dropped non-Latin characters in customer names, producing blank fields on printed invoices for several accounts before a support ticket caught it.

Katowice hit the same off-by-a-day stock count problem Rotterdam had, two weeks after that fix shipped. Katowice's reconciliation job runs through a legacy adapter that predates the read-time normalisation, so it never received the fix.

Replenishment model kept underforecasting demand for seasonal SKUs, so retrained it on eighteen months of sales history instead of six. The old window didn't span a full seasonal cycle, so it had never seen last year's equivalent spike.

Nordwind Fasteners shipped late on eleven of their last fourteen orders this quarter. Raised the safety-stock buffer for their SKUs from three days to ten days to absorb the delay until they sort out their side.

Decided the SKU catalog is the single source of truth for product weight and dimensions. The pricing engine and the carrier-rate calculator should both read those fields from the catalog at request time instead of keeping their own cached copies.

Pricing engine's currency conversion uses the previous day's ECB reference rate, refreshed at 06:00 UTC. Intraday rate swings aren't reflected until the next refresh, which finance has accepted as fine for display prices.

Picking app showed several SKUs as available when the shelf was actually empty. Traced it to the stock-count cache, which only reconciles against the warehouse floor every ten minutes because the sync job batches its writes instead of streaming them.

Added a real-time decrement to the picking app's count cache whenever a pick is confirmed, but only for high-velocity SKUs, the top few hundred by daily units moved. Low-velocity SKUs keep the ten-minute batch sync since the exposure is smaller.

Picking app tablets kept dropping their Bluetooth pairing with the handheld scanners mid-shift. A firmware update on the scanners fixed the drop; unrelated to the stock-count accuracy work, just an annoying disconnect bug.

Found non-EU shipments were being taxed at a flat EU-wide VAT rate instead of the destination country's actual rate, undercharging customers in several countries. Tax calculation now pulls the destination rate from a nightly-refreshed rates table.

Inbound QC now quarantines any pallet with visible crush damage before it reaches putaway, instead of the receiving clerk writing it off on the spot. A supervisor reviews quarantined pallets daily and decides scrap versus discount-sell.

Even after the retrain, holiday-adjacent SKUs still underforecast because the model has no signal for one-off promotions. Added a manual override list that planners fill in before promo weeks so the replenishment job doesn't undersupply them.

Returns portal now lets shoppers print a prepaid return label themselves instead of emailing support first. Average time from return request to label issued dropped from about two days to under ten minutes.

Orders placed within a two-hour window to the same delivery address are now batched into a single pick wave instead of being picked and packed separately. Cuts packaging material per order and reduces dock trips for local deliveries.

Route planning software now groups the next day's delivery stops by postcode district each morning rather than by order sequence. Drivers cover about fifteen percent less distance on average; unrelated to how orders get picked or packed.

Loading dock scanners were misreading barcodes printed on the older thermal ribbon stock, especially after the print head wore down partway through a roll. Switched to a higher-contrast ribbon after a two-week spike in manual re-scans.

Picking app tablets got a new home-screen layout putting the scan button within thumb reach. Minor usability tweak requested by the floor staff after a walkthrough on the floor, no functional change to scanning or stock accuracy at all.

Raised the write-off threshold for damaged goods from fifty to a hundred fifty dollars per unit. Finance found the approval workflow for small write-offs was costing more in reviewer time than the goods themselves were worth.

Low-stock alert threshold changed from a flat count of ten units to a formula based on average daily sales times three. Fast-moving SKUs now page someone with more lead time, and slow movers stop triggering alerts nobody acts on.

Low-stock alerts moved from email to a dedicated Slack channel. Median time from alert to someone acknowledging it dropped from around four hours to under twenty minutes, and the noise is easier to triage as a team.

Replenishment job's nightly query was taking forty seconds per warehouse and delaying the downstream reorder emails. Added an index on warehouse_id and it dropped to about three seconds; no change to what the job actually decides to reorder.

Found the carrier-rate calculator was still reading dimensions from a snapshot taken before the SKU catalog became the source of truth. Any SKU resized since March got quoted with stale numbers, undercharging shipping on oversized items for about two months.

Carrier's EDI feed started rejecting our shipment confirmations with an invalid weight unit error after a change on their side quietly defaulted to kilograms. Fixed by making the unit explicit in every payload instead of relying on their default.

Rotated the carrier account API credentials as part of the routine quarterly security review. No functional change, just the scheduled rotation that happens on this same cadence every quarter regardless of anything else going on.

Nordwind's late shipments this spring traced back to a carrier they'd switched to in January. They moved back to their original carrier in May and on-time delivery has been steady since, so the safety-stock buffer for their SKUs is back down to four days.

Quarter-end physical count came in 0.3% off from system stock, well within the accepted tolerance band. No root-cause investigation opened; logged as normal variance for the quarter and reviewed briefly in the ops sync.

Moved high-value SKUs from weekly to twice-weekly cycle counts. Even though the quarter-end variance was within tolerance, catching drift on the expensive items sooner seemed worth the extra counting time.

A gift-card SKU oversold badly during last week's promo because it sat in the low-velocity tier and only got the ten-minute batch sync. Extended the real-time decrement to every SKU, not just the high-velocity ones; the batch tier is retired.

Added a temporary night shift for the six weeks around peak season. The day shift alone couldn't clear the backlog of outbound orders once volume ramped up, and overtime on the day shift was hitting diminishing returns.

Trialled a four-day compressed work week outside of peak season. Ended it after five weeks: productivity on the fourth day dropped enough that total weekly output was about the same as five normal days.

Rotterdam's per-aisle stock view, requested back in March, shipped as a trial. It refreshes every fifteen minutes rather than in real time, which is fine for a read-only dashboard even with the picking app's earlier phantom-stock issue: nobody picks against this screen.
